q: What minimum share of the transmission capacity must TSOs make available for cross-zonal trade?
reference: For borders using a coordinated net transmission capacity approach “the minimum capacity shall be 70 % of the transmission capacity respecting operational security limits after deduction of contingencies”; for flow-based borders the margin “shall be 70 % of the capacity respecting operational security limits of internal and cross-zonal critical network elements”. “The total amount of 30 % can be used for the reliability margins, loop flows and internal flows on each critical network element.”

q: When may non-market-based redispatching of generation, energy storage and demand response be used?
reference: Only where “no market-based alternative is available”, “all available market-based resources have been used”, “the number of available power generating, energy storage or demand response facilities is too low to ensure effective competition” in the area where suitable facilities are located, or “the current grid situation leads to congestion in such a regular and predictable way that market-based redispatching would lead to regular strategic bidding which would increase the level of internal congestion”, and in that last case only if the Member State “either has adopted an action plan to address this congestion or ensures that minimum available capacity for cross-zonal trade is in accordance with Article 16(8)”.

q: Is there a maximum or minimum limit on the wholesale electricity price?
reference: “There shall be neither a maximum nor a minimum limit to the wholesale electricity price”, including for balancing energy and imbalance prices. That is “without prejudice to the technical price limits” that may be applied in the balancing timeframe (TSOs may propose harmonised maximum and minimum balancing energy prices, Reg. 2017/2195 Art. 30(2)) and, via NEMOs, harmonised limits on clearing prices in the day-ahead and intraday timeframes, which “shall be sufficiently high so as not to unnecessarily restrict trade”.

q: How much cross-zonal capacity may be allocated through the market-based allocation process for the exchange of balancing capacity?
reference: “Cross-zonal capacity allocated on a market-based process shall be limited to 10 % of the available capacity for the exchange of energy of the previous relevant calendar year between the respective bidding zones”; for new interconnectors the limit is “10 % of the total installed technical capacity of those new interconnectors”. This volume limitation “may not apply where the contracting is done not more than two days in advance of the provision of the balancing capacity or for bidding zone borders connected through DC interconnectors until the co-optimised allocation process is harmonised at Union level pursuant to Article 38(3)”.

q: What lower bound applies to the imbalance price for a negative imbalance?
reference: “The imbalance price for negative imbalance shall not be less than” either “the weighted average price for positive activated balancing energy from frequency restoration reserves and replacement reserves” or, if no balancing energy was activated in either direction in the period, the value of the avoided activation of balancing energy.

q: On what basis is the price of redispatching and countertrading resources determined?
reference: Pricing of redispatching and countertrading “shall be based on: (a) prices in the relevant electricity markets for the relevant time-frame; or (b) the cost of redispatching and countertrading resources calculated transparently on the basis of incurred costs.”

q: By when must the minimum cross-zonal capacity be reached, and how must capacity grow until then?
reference: “That minimum capacity shall be reached by 31 December 2025.” Until then, cross-zonal trade capacity is increased every year, and “those annual increases shall be achieved by means of a linear trajectory”.

q: How are the common costs of the European balancing platforms divided between countries and TSOs?
reference: “one eighth of the common cost shall be divided equally between each Member State and third country, five eighths shall be divided between each Member State and third country proportionally to their consumption, and two eighths shall be divided equally between the participating TSOs”.

q: How often must the value of lost load be updated, and by whom?
reference: Regulatory authorities, or other designated competent authorities, “shall update their estimate of the value of lost load at least every five years, or earlier where they observe a significant change”.

q: Must transmission system operators always implement the coordinated actions issued by regional coordination centres?
reference: No. They “shall implement the coordinated actions except where the implementation of the coordinated actions would result in a violation of the operational security limits” they have defined; a TSO that does not implement an action must “transparently report the detailed reasons” to the regional coordination centre and the other TSOs.

q: How must the imbalance netting power interchanges of all participating TSOs add up?
reference: “All TSOs participating in the same imbalance netting process shall ensure that the sum of all imbalance netting power interchanges is equal to zero.”

q: Which capacity calculation approach is the default for the day-ahead and intraday timeframes?
reference: “the approach used in the common capacity calculation methodologies shall be a flow-based approach, except where the requirement under paragraph 7 is met”; under paragraph 7 TSOs may jointly request the competent regulatory authorities to apply the coordinated net transmission capacity approach in regions and bidding zone borders other than those referred to in paragraphs 2 to 4, if they demonstrate that flow-based “would not yet be more efficient” than that approach at the same operational security.

q: Can a balancing service provider still update its balancing energy bid after gate closure?
reference: No. “After the balancing energy gate closure time, the balancing service providers shall no longer be permitted to submit or update their balancing energy bids.”

q: How soon after transfer must congestion income be distributed under the sharing methodology?
reference: TSOs distribute congestion incomes “as soon as reasonably practicable and no later than one week after the congestion incomes have been transferred”.

q: May a transmission operator hold back cross-border transfer capacity from the market in order to relieve a bottleneck located within its own price area?
reference: No. TSOs “shall not limit the volume of interconnection capacity to be made available to market participants as a means of solving congestion inside their own bidding zone or as a means of managing flows resulting from transactions internal to bidding zones”; this applies without prejudice to the derogations under paragraphs 3 and 9 (operational security), and is considered complied with where minimum levels of 70 % of capacity respecting operational security limits are made available.

q: How often is there a European report on lasting grid bottlenecks within and between price areas?
reference: “Every three years, the ENTSO for Electricity shall report on structural congestions and other major physical congestions between and within bidding zones”, including their location and frequency.

q: A wind farm is switched off by the grid operator without a market mechanism. Is the owner compensated?
reference: Yes. Non-market-based redispatching “shall be subject to financial compensation by the system operator requesting the redispatching”, except for producers that have accepted a connection agreement with no guarantee of firm delivery. The compensation must be at least equal to the higher of (a) the additional operating cost and (b) the “net revenues from the sale of electricity on the day-ahead market” the facility would otherwise have generated, “or a combination of both if applying only the higher would lead to an unjustifiably low or an unjustifiably high compensation”.

q: What can the money earned from scarce cross-border transmission capacity be spent on?
reference: Revenues from allocating cross-zonal capacity have three priority objectives (Art. 19(2)): “guaranteeing the actual availability of the allocated capacity including firmness compensation”; “maintaining or increasing cross-zonal capacities” (by optimising existing interconnectors through coordinated remedial actions or covering relevant network investment costs); or “compensating offshore renewable electricity generation plant operators in an offshore bidding zone directly connected to two or more bidding zones where access to interconnected markets has been reduced”. Where these have been adequately fulfilled, the revenues may be taken into account by regulators when approving network tariffs, and “the residual revenues shall be placed on a separate internal account line” until they can be spent on those purposes.

q: May a third-party firm that bundles households' flexible consumption and sells it on electricity markets do so without its customers' energy retailer agreeing?
reference: No. The regulatory framework must contain “the right for each market participant engaged in aggregation, including independent aggregators, to enter electricity markets without the consent of other market participants”, and customers with an independent aggregator must not face “undue payments, penalties or other undue contractual restrictions by their suppliers”.

q: Which regional organisations replaced the regional security coordinators, and from when did they have to operate?
reference: The regional coordination centres “shall replace the regional security coordinators” and “shall enter into operation by 1 July 2022”, following approval by the regulatory authorities of the TSOs' proposal under paragraph 1.

q: What must national law let local-network operators do, and what must it give them, when they would rather purchase services from nearby generators, storage or demand response than upgrade their lines?
reference: “Member States shall provide the necessary regulatory framework to allow and provide incentives to distribution system operators to procure flexibility services, including congestion management in their areas”; the framework must ensure DSOs “are able to procure such services from providers of distributed generation, demand response or energy storage” where the services “cost-effectively alleviate the need to upgrade or replace electricity capacity”.

q: By default, how far ahead of delivery may reserve capacity be contracted, and for how long may such contracts run?
reference: By default, “Contracts for balancing capacity shall not be concluded more than one day before the provision of the balancing capacity and the contracting period shall be no longer than one day”. Only if the regulatory authority approves a derogation may this be relaxed: at least 40 % of standard balancing products and 30 % of all balancing-capacity products must still follow the one-day rule, while “The contracting of the remaining part of the balancing capacity shall be performed for a maximum of one month in advance of the provision of balancing capacity and shall have a maximum contractual period of one month”; the regulatory authority may extend that to “a maximum period of twelve months”, but “from 1 January 2026 contract periods shall not be longer than six months”.

q: Which technical parameters define a harmonised balancing energy bid, for instance how quickly the resource must reach full output?
reference: The list of standard products may set out characteristics such as the “preparation period”, “ramping period”, “full activation time”, minimum and maximum quantity, “deactivation period”, minimum and maximum duration of delivery period, validity period and “mode of activation”.

q: After which market deadlines must the cross-border capacity available to traders be recomputed?
reference: “Transmission system operators shall recalculate available cross-zonal capacity at least after day-ahead gate closure times and after intraday cross-zonal gate closure times.”

q: What options exist for setting aside border transmission capacity for the exchange of reserves?
reference: TSOs may propose one of three processes: “co-optimised allocation process pursuant to Article 40”, “market-based allocation process pursuant to Article 41” or “allocation process based on economic efficiency analysis pursuant to Article 42”.

q: If the price charged for deviations from schedule falls below zero, does a balance responsible party that ended up with a surplus receive money or have to pay?
reference: It has to pay. A surplus is a positive imbalance (“a positive sign, indicating a balance responsible party's surplus”), and when the imbalance price is negative a positive imbalance is “Payment from BRP to TSO”.

q: Must a balancing resource and the party responsible for its imbalances sit in the same scheduling area?
reference: Yes. For each product for balancing energy or balancing capacity, the reserve providing unit, group, demand facility or third party and the associated balance responsible parties “shall belong to the same scheduling area”.

q: Who decides between introducing an action plan and redrawing price zones when a lasting bottleneck is identified, and what happens if countries cannot agree?
reference: The Member State with identified structural congestion shall, with its TSOs, “decide, within six months of receipt of the report, either to establish national or multinational action plans pursuant to Article 15, or to review and amend its bidding zone configuration”. If relevant Member States fail to agree unanimously on an amendment within six months they notify the Commission, which decides “as a measure of last resort” after consulting ACER.

q: Is it a requirement that the fees generators or consumers pay for using the grid differ according to where they connect, and what should those fees reflect?
reference: Not always, only “Where appropriate”: “Where appropriate, the level of the tariffs applied to producers or final customers, or to both shall provide locational investment signals at Union level, such as incentives via tariff structure to reduce re-dispatching and power grid reinforcement costs and take into account the amount of network losses and congestion caused, and investment costs for infrastructure.”

q: Is a grid operator allowed to leave a network overload unresolved, rather than pay for corrective measures, if its effects stay within its own area and no joint handling with neighbouring operators is needed?
reference: Yes. Where constraints “have only consequences on the local state within the TSO's control area and the operational security violation does not need to be managed in a coordinated way, the TSO responsible for its management may decide not to activate remedial actions with costs to relieve them”.

q: What criteria guide a TSO when choosing between possible grid-security countermeasures?
reference: A TSO must “activate the most effective and economically efficient remedial actions”, “activate remedial actions as close as possible to real-time”, consider the risks of failure, and “give preference to remedial actions which make available the largest cross-zonal capacity for capacity allocation, while satisfying all operational security limits”.

q: Whose task is it to collect the revenue generated by scarce interconnection capacity?
reference: Each transmission system operator is responsible for “collecting congestion rents and payments under the inter-transmission system operator compensation mechanism”.

q: When a grid operator needs to cut back forward-allocated cross-border capacity more than 48 hours before the delivery day, which body works out the required cuts?
reference: The responsible coordinated capacity calculator, at the request of the TSO needing the cut: that TSO “shall send a request to the responsible coordinated capacity calculator to launch the coordinated calculation of necessary curtailments of long-term cross-zonal capacity for the capacity calculation region”. This coordinated route applies to curtailments more than 48 hours ahead; within 48 hours TSOs “shall apply the day-ahead and intraday capacity calculation process”.

q: When a transmission operator withdraws interconnector capacity in an emergency that participants bought in stand-alone capacity auctions (separately from energy), what are those participants entitled to receive?
reference: In an emergency situation with explicit allocation, market participants “shall be entitled to compensation equal to the price difference of relevant markets between the bidding zones concerned in the relevant time-frame”; where no bidding zone price is calculated in one of the two zones they are entitled to “reimbursement of the price paid for capacity during the explicit allocation process”.

q: Once structural congestion has been identified, what must the Member State decide within six months, and, if it opts for an action plan, by what date must the minimum cross-zonal capacity be reached?
reference: The Member State must “decide, within six months of receipt of the report, either to establish national or multinational action plans pursuant to Article 15, or to review and amend its bidding zone configuration” (Art. 14(7)); under an action plan “that minimum capacity shall be reached by 31 December 2025” (Art. 15(2)).

q: Which body facilitates the regional procurement of balancing capacity, and what may it do as a last resort when the available remedial actions cannot deliver the minimum capacity?
reference: Regional coordination centres are tasked with “facilitating the regional procurement of balancing capacity” (Art. 37(1)(k)); where available remedial actions are insufficient, “they may, as a measure of last resort, set out coordinated actions reducing the cross-zonal capacities accordingly” (Art. 16(3)).

q: How must the resources redispatched to relieve congestion be selected, and what is the only additional charge allowed for exchanging balancing energy across borders?
reference: Redispatched resources “shall be selected from among generating facilities, energy storage or demand response using market-based mechanisms and shall be financially compensated” (Reg. 2019/943 Art. 13(2)); the cross-zonal pricing methodology must “not apply any additional charges for the exchange of balancing energy or for operating the imbalance netting process, except a charge to compensate losses” (Reg. 2017/2195 Art. 30(3)(c)).

q: Which allocation processes can set aside border capacity for balancing, and how large a share of the previous year's capacity can the market-based one use?
reference: Two or more TSOs may propose applying a “co-optimised allocation process”, a “market-based allocation process” or an “allocation process based on economic efficiency analysis” (Art. 38(1)); the market-based one “shall be limited to 10 % of the available capacity for the exchange of energy of the previous relevant calendar year” between the respective bidding zones (10 % of installed technical capacity for new interconnectors), though the limit “may not apply where the contracting is done not more than two days in advance” of the provision of the balancing capacity (Art. 41(2)).

q: Who pays for the remedial actions needed to reach the cross-zonal capacity trajectory, and how must the cost-sharing methodology treat redispatching with cross-border relevance?
reference: The cost of the remedial actions “shall be borne by the Member State or Member States implementing the action plan” (Reg. 2019/943 Art. 15(3)); the redispatching and countertrading cost sharing methodology “shall include cost-sharing solutions for actions of cross-border relevance” (Reg. 2015/1222 Art. 74(2)).

q: With whom must a TSO coordinate when preparing a redispatching measure, and what may it not do on its own for redispatching of cross-border relevance?
reference: The TSO must assess the impact of the measure “in coordination with the TSOs concerned” (Reg. 2017/1485 Art. 23(2)) and, where it affects transmission-connected SGUs and DSOs, “in coordination with the affected SGUs and DSOs” (Art. 23(3)); and “each TSO shall abstain from unilateral or uncoordinated redispatching and countertrading measures of cross-border relevance” (Reg. 2015/1222 Art. 35(4)).

q: Is an aggregator of demand response financially liable for the imbalances it causes, and how may it organise its balance responsibility?
reference: Yes. Member States must ensure the framework contains “an obligation on market participants engaged in aggregation to be financially responsible for the imbalances that they cause in the electricity system”; aggregators “shall be balance responsible parties or shall delegate their balancing responsibility” in accordance with Article 5 of Regulation 2019/943.

q: Which bodies perform regional sizing of reserve capacity, and what lower bound, relative to the dimensioning incident, applies to the positive FRR reserve capacity of an LFC block?
reference: Regional coordination centres carry out “regional sizing of reserve capacity” (Reg. 2019/943 Art. 37(1)(j)); the positive reserve capacity on FRR “shall not be less than the positive dimensioning incident of the LFC block” (Reg. 2017/1485 Art. 157(2)(e)), although a FRR sharing agreement may reduce it (in the CE and Nordic areas by at most 30 % of the positive dimensioning incident, Art. 157(2)(j)).

q: How do two-sided contracts for difference change the revenue of renewable generators under the 2024 electricity market reform?
reference: A “two-way contract for difference” is a contract between a power-generating facility operator and a counterpart, usually a public entity, that “provides both minimum remuneration protection and a limit to excess remuneration” (Art. 2(76)).
